Two sigma is a move bigger than roughly 95% of its last twenty sessions — rare enough to be information rather than noise. A 1.8% day on the S&P is ordinary in a volatile month and remarkable in a calm one; sigma is what tells the difference.

The Nasdaq −2.60% at 2.43σ is its largest move in the 29 sessions on this board, and gold −2.81% at 2.36σ is right behind it. The indices, precisely. The Nasdaq fell 694.00 points to 26,008.86 and the S&P 93.74 to 7,663.43, its worst day since July. The Dow rose 11.89 to 52,867.98 and the Russell 3.01 to 2,784.03 — so most US stocks actually rose, and the technology losses were heavy enough to hide it. The semiconductor index fell more than 6% to about 10,690, just above its 200-day average near 10,677. Technology fell 3.3% and communications 1.4%, while consumer staples rose more than 3% and utilities, health care, property and financials each about 1% or more; homebuilders and mortgage names rallied as yields fell. The VIX touched 20.30 intraday, up more than 21% at one point, but stayed below its 22.31 high of 16 October. Week to date: Russell +2.3%, Dow +1.7%, S&P +0.1%, Nasdaq −0.5%. For the year: Dow +10.0%, Russell +12.2%, S&P +11.9%, Nasdaq +11.9%.

The bond rally is the largest single move on this page. The ten-year fell about 18 basis points to 4.95% — its biggest one-day drop since August 2025, and a long way from the 5.3645% it printed on 7 October. The five-year fell about 18bp to 4.77%, the two-year about 16bp to 4.65% and the thirty-year about 13bp to 5.29%. Because the front end fell further than the long, the spread between two years and thirty widened to about 64 basis points from 61 — three sessions of flattening undone in one. The market now puts only about a 10.5% chance of a hike at the 27-28 October meeting, though the CME tool still has roughly 86% on a December increase, and Goldman Sachs expects one more quarter-point then, to a 4.00-4.25% peak. Initial jobless claims fell to 194,000, the lowest in three months, so none of this was about the labour market.

And France went past the United States. The ten-year OAT rose six basis points to 5.06%, a fresh 24-year high, while the US ten-year fell — and for the first time since the 2013 euro-area debt crisis a French government bond yields more than an American one. French debt is heading for about 120% of GDP. Economist Robin Brooks reads much of the sell-off as a positioning unwind: foreign investors who bought French debt heavily over the summer — June 2026 was the largest foreign inflow on record — are scaling back. Joseph Brusuelas argues ECB backstops encouraged carry trades into riskier euro-area sovereigns, and expects volatility until the French election next April settles fiscal policy.

Commodities went the other way from everything else. Brent rose 4% to $113.17 and WTI $2.32 or 2.39% to $99.47, a five-month high. Gold fell 2.81% to $4,024.82, its lowest since early August, and silver 4.68% to $55.01 — which is the uncomfortable combination: an oil shock that lifts inflation expectations while a bond rally says growth, and gold sold by both. Bitcoin fell below $82,000. And China's CSI 300 closed in a bear market, 20.2% below its 22 June peak at 4,036.30.

Cash is not a position, but on this particular Thursday it behaved like a very good one.

Wednesday's answer lasted nineteen hours

1. Meta's filing, not Meta's earnings, broke the AI trade. On Wednesday night the numbers looked like a vindication: revenue $64.60bn, up 26%, the 2026 capex floor raised to $135bn, and the shares up about 3% after hours. On Thursday a filing showed future commitments — mostly computing power and data-centre leases — well above their July level, total expense guidance went to $175-179bn, and the stock fell 6.98% to $648.85. Nothing in the results changed. What changed is that the market read the balance-sheet commitment rather than the income statement, and decided that $34.9bn of quarterly capex producing negative $2.12bn of free cash flow is a liability and not an investment. Meta ended the quarter with $82.4bn of cash against $83.7bn of debt, and the chief financial officer said there were no financing plans to announce.

2. And the distinction the market drew is the one Alphabet has to answer on the 28th. Meta funds its data centres out of advertising. Alphabet and Microsoft also rent capacity to outside customers, which is the structural defence: the spending is supposed to arrive back as cloud revenue. Except that on Wednesday Pichai said that cloud revenue is being deliberately held back to give DeepMind capacity, with new customers next year incredibly difficult. So the defence has been qualified by the company that owns it, six days before it reports. Alphabet fell 3.08% and Microsoft 1.5% while the semiconductor index fell more than 6% and Lam Research 9% on weak guidance. The chain is coherent: if the hyperscalers' spending is a liability, the people selling them equipment have a demand problem.

3. The bond market took the other side, and France went past the United States. The ten-year fell about 18 basis points to 4.95%, its largest one-day drop since August 2025, with the two-year down about 16 and the thirty-year 13. Hike odds for next week fell to about 10.5%. That is not an inflation trade — crude rose 2.4% on the same afternoon — it is money leaving equity risk and a growth scare being priced, with jobless claims at 194,000, a three-month low, ruling out the labour market as the cause. Meanwhile the French ten-year rose 6bp to 5.06%, a 24-year high, and crossed above the US ten-year for the first time since 2013. This brief spent Monday to Wednesday establishing that French politics does not move American yields. Thursday confirmed it from the opposite direction: the two curves moved apart as far as they have in thirteen years, in a single session, for entirely unrelated reasons.

The strikes now have a date, and it is after the midterms

The New York Times reported that the United States and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the 3 November midterms. The reported target set is energy sites, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenals, with the report allowing a small chance that it happens this month. Trump said the US is not negotiating with Iran and that something will happen fairly soon; a separate report had the Israeli chief of staff seeing no operational need to strike before the election. That is the first time this conflict has had a date attached to it, and a dated war is a different instrument from an open-ended one — it gives the oil curve something to price rather than something to fear.

Crude priced it immediately. Brent rose $4.35, or 4%, to $113.17 and WTI $2.32, or 2.39%, to $99.47, a five-month high, after touching $100. The other half of the move was physical: an attack on King Fahd International Airport at Dammam killed one resident and injured eight, per Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority, and there were further reported strikes on Saudi energy targets. The IRGC Navy said four oil-carrying vessels were hit and caught fire in the northern Persian Gulf, and three more struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, and warned that continued US escorting of ships through the Strait could bring responses against American regional bases.

And then the strangest line of the day. Trump accused Iran of making up fake hits on ships to drive up oil prices ahead of the midterms. Take it seriously as market information rather than as rhetoric: it is an American president publicly asserting that part of the war premium in the oil price is fabricated, eight days after signing an order waiving sanctions on Russian energy to hold fuel prices down, and twelve days before an election. Whether or not the claim is true, it tells you the energy line in the inflation data is now being managed as a political variable, and that the administration's tolerance for a hundred-dollar barrel before 3 November is low.

For this book the transmission has changed shape. A fortnight ago crude rising meant yields rising, and that was the whole mechanism — energy into inflation into the long end into everything. On Thursday crude rose 2.4% and the ten-year fell 18 basis points. The bond market has stopped treating the oil shock as an inflation problem and started treating it as a demand one, which is the same conclusion the housing data forced on Tuesday. Gold fell 2.81% on the same afternoon, which only makes sense if the market is pricing growth damage rather than price pressure. If that holds, the energy premium stops being the thing that threatens this book's valuations and becomes the thing that threatens its earnings.

Four of six instruments had a move of more than one weekly sigma, and the ranking is the whole week. The Russell fell 3.05% at 3.17σ — the largest weekly reading on this board in the series. The Nasdaq fell 4.48% at 1.99σ, crude rose 11.73% at 1.85σ and the S&P fell 1.95% at 1.69σ. And then the two that did nothing: the Dow rose 0.67% at 0.63σ and gold fell 0.20% at 0.13σ. A week in which the small-cap index has its most unusual move of the series, the Nasdaq has its worst week since June, crude rises eleven percent and gold does not move at all is not a week with one story in it.

The indices, precisely. Across the five sessions the S&P fell 152.10 points, or 1.9%, to 7,659.44; the Nasdaq 1,226.14, or 4.5%, to 26,140.03 — its worst week since June, as was the S&P's; the Russell 85.61, or 3%, to 2,721.37. The Dow rose 347.46 points, or 0.7%, to 52,002.41, and was the only index up. For the year the S&P is now up 11.9%, the Nasdaq 12.5%, the Russell 9.6% and the Dow 8.2% — the Dow has closed almost the whole of the gap the Nasdaq built over the first nine months.

Two first-tier prints, both hot, and the long end fell anyway. September CPI on Wednesday came in +0.6% on the month and +3.7% on the year, core +0.3% and +2.6%, both above forecast — with gasoline +9.1% and +34.2% doing over half the monthly increase on the BLS's own reckoning, and shelter and core services both accelerating to +0.4%. September PPI on Thursday came in at +1.3% against +0.5% expected, +6.3% on the year, with energy goods +10.8% and gasoline +20.3% at the producer level. Hike odds for 28 October went from about 22% to roughly 50% to about 27% inside three sessions. And the ten-year finished the week about 14 basis points lower and the thirty-year about 17, at 5.43%. Fed Chair Warsh's IMF remarks left roughly an 85% hold priced for this month.

The number that explains it is in the retail sales report, not the inflation ones. Headline retail sales rose 0.8% against 0.3% expected, to $745.0bn. But the control group rose only 0.1% against 0.3% expected, and excluding petrol stations the increase was 0.2%. So the consumer is not spending more; the consumer is paying more for fuel. Gasoline did over half of CPI, rose a fifth at the producer level, and supplied most of the retail beat. The bond market read that as a tax on demand rather than inflation to be met with hikes, and bought duration into two hot prints. That is the single most important thing the week established.

And crude broke a hundred dollars. WTI went from $90.76 to $101.41, +11.7%, and Brent from $103.35 to $109.86, touching $110 on Friday for the first time since May. Gold finished the week almost exactly where it started, at $4,166.39, having fallen 1.34% on the CPI and risen 1.60% on the PPI. An eleven-percent week in oil and a flat week in gold is a market pricing a supply problem, not a monetary one.

The 5 October valuation note has now largely been settled against the position.

PLTR gave back everything, and AAPL was the only thing that worked. Palantir fell 11.0% from the all-time closing high of 209.05 it set on 9 October, and on Friday traded down to 184.45 — within a cent of the entry — before closing at +0.08R. It fell 4.7% across the week, from 262.43 to 250.00, costing −37.29 — and still accounts for 79% of the +131.02 held open, at +5.17R. That share rose over a week in which the position lost money, because everything else lost more. Its stop sits at the fill, which protects every dollar of capital and none of the gain, and after a week like this one that is the only decision still outstanding in this book.

Where the quarter stands · twelve sessions in

Q4 is +131.02 at +6.55R, of which none is realised: it is open profit accrued since entry, not a Q4 return. Q3 finished at +17.04, +0.84R, against the S&P's +2.0%. On $1,335.73 of capital still committed the open book is +9.81% since entry. The week cost -98.36 against an S&P down 1.9%, a Nasdaq down 4.5% and a Dow up 0.7%, which is the comparison that matters: 2 of the 4 positions are above +1R (AAPL at +1.08R, AMZN at +5.17R), and the index this book owns nothing in was the only one that rose.

Two hot prints, a bank fine, a foldable sell-out, and a rotation that completed

1. The long end fell through two hot inflation prints, and that settles a three-week argument. The thesis built from 29 September was that the long end was rising on supply and global debt rather than inflation. This week tested it to destruction: the ten-year spiked to 5.33% on the CPI and closed back at 5.19%; then fell 12 basis points on the PPI to a three-week low; and finished the week about 14 basis points lower, with the thirty-year 17 lower at 5.43%. Neither explanation survives. An inflation trade would have risen and stayed risen. A pure supply trade would not have spiked on CPI at all. What fits is the retail sales control group at +0.1%: the market read energy-driven price rises as demand destruction and bought duration into them. Hike odds for 28 October ended the week near 27% after touching 50%.

2. The banks reported and the split told you where the cycle is. JPMorgan missed for the first time in nearly three years — $5.57 against $5.93 expected — on investment banking and a fixed-income desk that slowed from the summer. Goldman earned $17.01 against $12.25 a year ago on stock trading, with bond trading slower. Citigroup's profit rose 40% but card profits were flat. Bank of America missed on Wednesday — $0.91 a share including a charge, $1.08 against $1.10 excluding it, revenue $30bn against $30.58bn, investment banking fees −11% and sales and trading −5% — the day after the Treasury fined it $1.2bn, the third-largest penalty in that department's history, for willful Bank Secrecy Act violations involving more than $5bn of suspicious transactions. The pattern: equity desks busy, bond desks quiet, consumer flat.

3. Apple's foldable sold out in minutes, which was the only checkable fact in a fortnight of sourcing. Three parties had disagreed from anonymous supply-chain contacts — Nikkei on iPhone 18 Pro cuts, Securities Times on Duo orders raised 30% toward ten million units, Bank of America on shorter Pro delivery times — and Friday replaced all of it with evidence. Pre-orders opened at 8am Eastern, stock went within moments, shipping slipped to late January 2027 on some configurations, Apple called demand nothing short of extraordinary, and units resold at up to $5,000 against a $1,999 list. The fair caveat is that a sell-out is a ratio and Apple probably built few of them. The resale premium is harder to argue with.

4. And the rotation completed, which is the week's real lesson for this book. Over five sessions the Dow rose 0.7% and was the only index up, while the Nasdaq fell 4.5% and the Russell 3%. Friday's sell-off is the one to study: the Nasdaq fell 2.15% and the Dow 0.34% while the ten-year rose two basis points. That was not a rate event. Micron fell 5.6% and Intel 5.8% as investors grew more concerned about how long AI infrastructure spending will last, and Okta, Palantir, Datadog, Zscaler and Elastic were sold together. A rate scare reverses when the Fed is repriced — and it did, on Thursday. A thesis under question does not.

Crude rose eleven percent through two emergency releases

WTI went from $90.76 to $101.41 across the week, up 11.7%, and Brent touched $110 on Friday for the first time since May. It did so through four separate supply events and against the two largest tools short of policy that the agencies have. Monday: +3.28% on renewed Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Tuesday: WTI up, Brent down, as traders weighed a possible US–Russia diesel deal against escalation in Yemen. Wednesday: +1.01% after a Houthi missile hit an office tower at Aramco's Dhahran headquarters — top three floors damaged, limited fire, no injuries, a command centre rather than a producing asset. Thursday: +3.03% on a US inventory draw. Friday: +3.51%.

Friday's reasons are worth separating because one of them is new. A Saudi-led coalition intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Yanbu — the Red Sea export terminal whose entire strategic value is that crude leaving from it bypasses the Strait of Hormuz. Targeting the hedge against the chokepoint is an escalation in kind, not degree. Ukrainian strikes also damaged the Ryazan refinery, shutting a primary crude unit, which bears directly on Russian diesel. And the EIA reported US crude stocks down 8.6m barrels to 415.6m, with distillates down 2.5m.

Against all of which: the IEA announced the release of over 20m barrels of emergency supply, and Washington offered up to 17m through a reserve exchange. Roughly 37m barrels of announced additional supply, and the price rose 3.5% on the day and 11.7% on the week. The reason is the number Aramco's Amin Nasser has been repeating: commercial inventory under 6 billion barrels against roughly 10 billion before the crisis, with less than 10% practically available and up to two years to rebuild. A release needs a cushion to land on. There is not one.

And the diesel number is how all of this reaches a book with no oil position in it. The IEA reported combined net gasoil exports from the Middle East and Russia down 1.3m barrels a day in September to 820,000 — more than 60% lower year on year — with no stock rebuild expected before the second half of 2027, because the binding constraint is how much Russian refining capacity is actually running. Gulf crude exports are back at 13.9m barrels a day, over 75% of pre-war; refined product exports are 1.9m against 4.7m. Crude flows and product does not. That gap is why gasoline rose 20.3% at the producer level in September and did over half of the CPI increase — and the October print, due 10 November, carries a crude price eleven percent higher than when this week began.

There is nothing dated for ten days, and that has not been true since late September. No print, no earnings, no scheduled event from any company held, until the Duo ships on Friday 23 October. Then the calendar compresses: the Fed and Alphabet on Wednesday the 28th, Apple and Amazon on Thursday the 29th, Palantir on 2 November and October CPI on the 10th. Four of the five positions this book has held during October report inside those three days.

Alphabet on the 28th is the one that has changed character. A fortnight ago its $195-205bn of capex and the 3.6-gigawatt Constellation deal were the bull case — evidence of scale. After a Friday in which Micron fell 5.6% and Intel 5.8% because investors are no longer sure how long AI infrastructure spending lasts, the same number is the thing the print has to defend. And it lands the same afternoon the Fed decides, so two factors resolve on one day for a book exposed to both.

What to watch in this book. Whether AMZN holds at +5.17R, since it is 79% of the open profit with the gain entirely unprotected. Whether PLTR can stay above the entry it touched on Friday, at +0.08R. And whether OKTA finds a floor at +0.23R after nineteen percent in five sessions. All of them now turn on one question, and it is no longer the Fed: whether the market still believes the AI build.

The standing position: do nothing, because nothing can be done. Heat is 3.00R against a 3.0R cap and has not moved in twenty-seven sessions, so no position can be added however attractive anything looks. This week was the first real test of that constraint: two holdings fell more than ten percent, one closed, and the book could not respond to any of it. The ten days to the 23rd are the first stretch since September with nothing to react to, which makes them the right time to decide what this book should look like when it can act again.

items.html: Fell 3.08% to 320.76, a third consecutive lower close, on volume about 4% above average. Low 318.45. That is through the 328.38 of 9 September, which had been the lowest close of the past two months, and it happened inside the broadest AI de-rating of the month rather than on anything of its own: Meta fell 6.98%, Lam Research about 9%, CoreWeave 10% and the semiconductor index more than 6%.

The distinction the market drew is the one that matters for the 28th. Meta funds its data centres out of advertising; Alphabet and Microsoft also rent capacity to outside customers, which is supposed to make the spending self-financing. On Wednesday Pichai said that cloud revenue is being deliberately held back to feed frontier AI. So the one structural defence Alphabet had against Meta's problem is the thing its own chief executive has just qualified, six days before it reports.

Sundar Pichai said Google Cloud is forgoing short-term revenue to make compute trade-offs for frontier AI. On the Big Technology Podcast he called giving DeepMind enough capacity non-negotiable and said taking on new customers who need capacity for next year would be incredibly difficult. He put no number on it and gave no date for when added capacity reaches outside customers. The stock fell 1.62% that day while the Nasdaq rose 1.05%.

KeyCorp cut its target to $410 from $435 while keeping Overweight, and lead-plaintiff reminders in the securities class action put the deadline at 1 December. The 28 October print carries $195-205bn of capex and now lands the same afternoon as the Fed.

The Duo reaches shops in the US and more than seventy countries under a two-unit purchase limit, and Moody's reviews France at Aa3 negative with the OAT at a 24-year high and now yielding more than the Treasury. world.title: The strikes now have a date, and it is after the midterms
world.note: The New York Times reported that the United States and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the 3 November midterms. The reported target set is energy sites, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenals, with the report allowing a small chance that it happens this month. Trump said the US is not negotiating with Iran and that something will happen fairly soon; a separate report had the Israeli chief of staff seeing no operational need to strike before the election. That is the first time this conflict has had a date attached to it, and a dated war is a different instrument from an open-ended one — it gives the oil curve something to price rather than something to fear.

The Nasdaq −2.60% at 2.43σ is its largest move in the 29 sessions on this board, and gold −2.81% at 2.36σ is right behind it. A tape that records a two-sigma collapse in one index and a flat print in another on the same afternoon is not describing a market falling. changed.note: 1. Meta's filing, not Meta's earnings, broke the AI trade. On Wednesday night the numbers looked like a vindication: revenue $64.60bn, up 26%, the 2026 capex floor raised to $135bn, and the shares up about 3% after hours. What changed is that the market read the balance-sheet commitment rather than the income statement, and decided that $34.9bn of quarterly capex producing negative $2.12bn of free cash flow is a liability and not an investment. Meta ended the quarter with $82.4bn of cash against $83.7bn of debt, and the chief financial officer said there were no financing plans to announce.

And then the other half of the board did nothing at all: the Dow +0.02% at 0.04σ and the Russell +0.11% at 0.12σ. A tape that records a two-sigma collapse in one index and a flat print in another on the same afternoon is not describing a market falling. It is describing one trade being taken apart while everything else is bought with the proceeds.

The indices, precisely. The Nasdaq fell 694.00 points to 26,008.86 and the S&P 93.74 to 7,663.43, its worst day since July. The Dow rose 11.89 to 52,867.98 and the Russell 3.01 to 2,784.03 — so most US stocks actually rose, and the technology losses were heavy enough to hide it. The semiconductor index fell more than 6% to about 10,690, just above its 200-day average near 10,677. Technology fell 3.3% and communications 1.4%, while consumer staples rose more than 3% and utilities, health care, property and financials each about 1% or more; homebuilders and mortgage names rallied as yields fell. The VIX touched 20.30 intraday, up more than 21% at one point, but stayed below its 22.31 high of 16 October. Week to date: Russell +2.3%, Dow +1.7%, S&P +0.1%, Nasdaq −0.5%. For the year: Dow +10.0%, Russell +12.2%, S&P +11.9%, Nasdaq +11.9%.

The bond rally is the largest single move on this page. The ten-year fell about 18 basis points to 4.95% — its biggest one-day drop since August 2025, and a long way from the 5.3645% it printed on 7 October. The five-year fell about 18bp to 4.77%, the two-year about 16bp to 4.65% and the thirty-year about 13bp to 5.29%. Because the front end fell further than the long, the spread between two years and thirty widened to about 64 basis points from 61 — three sessions of flattening undone in one. The market now puts only about a 10.5% chance of a hike at the 27-28 October meeting, though the CME tool still has roughly 86% on a December increase, and Goldman Sachs expects one more quarter-point then, to a 4.00-4.25% peak. Initial jobless claims fell to 194,000, the lowest in three months, so none of this was about the labour market.

And France went past the United States. The ten-year OAT rose six basis points to 5.06%, a fresh 24-year high, while the US ten-year fell — and for the first time since the 2013 euro-area debt crisis a French government bond yields more than an American one. French debt is heading for about 120% of GDP. Economist Robin Brooks reads much of the sell-off as a positioning unwind: foreign investors who bought French debt heavily over the summer — June 2026 was the largest foreign inflow on record — are scaling back. Joseph Brusuelas argues ECB backstops encouraged carry trades into riskier euro-area sovereigns, and expects volatility until the French election next April settles fiscal policy.

Commodities went the other way from everything else. Brent rose 4% to $113.17 and WTI $2.32 or 2.39% to $99.47, a five-month high. Gold fell 2.81% to $4,024.82, its lowest since early August, and silver 4.68% to $55.01 — which is the uncomfortable combination: an oil shock that lifts inflation expectations while a bond rally says growth, and gold sold by both. Bitcoin fell below $82,000. And China's CSI 300 closed in a bear market, 20.2% below its 22 June peak at 4,036.30.

Three closed, one left, and 1.99R of room for the first time in a month

The three exits are the whole story of this book's month, so take them in order. AMZN went first, on 15 October at 250.28 — the stop had been moved to the fill, the stock opened below it, and the exit was the open rather than the stop: -4.68 at -0.23R. OKTA went on the 16th at 202.79, +20.06 and +1.00R — taken on the way down through a session that fell 10.20%, which is the hard version of the discipline rather than the easy one. AAPL went on the 19th at 341.23, +19.26 at +0.93R. Two taken at about one R, one small loss on a gap: +34.64 realised at +1.70R, against +39.32 from the two winners and -4.68 from the one that gapped.

What that bought is the thing this brief has been describing as impossible for twenty-nine sessions: room. Heat is 1.01R against a 3.0R cap, so 1.99R is unused. For a month every session ended with the same sentence — nothing can be added, the stops are where they were, the book can act in neither direction. That is no longer true. It became untrue in the week the AI complex de-rated, and on Thursday the index that complex sits in fell 2.60%, its largest single-session move in 29 sessions. Cash is not a position, but on this particular Thursday it behaved like a very good one.

And the one position left is the one with a problem. GOOG fell 3.08% to 320.76, a third consecutive lower close and through the 328.38 of 9 September that had been the lowest close of the past two months, with the low at 318.45. At -0.25R it is now below its 325.86 entry, having been +0.25R on Wednesday. It now sits 4.01% above the 305.67 stop on the day's low — the closest this position has come — and the 28 October print carrying $195-205bn of capex arrives in six days, into a market that has just spent a session punishing exactly that. The stop is where it was. It is the only thing standing between this book and a loss, and it does not need to be touched.

Q4 is +29.54 at +1.45R, and for the first time this quarter most of it is real. +34.64 is realised and banked, which no subsequent session can take away; the open position's -5.10 is the only part still moving. Q3 finished at +12.31, +0.58R, against the S&P's +2.0% — so this quarter is already 2.4 times Q3 with a week still to run, and the difference is not that the positions were better. It is that three of them were closed while they were still worth something. On the $325.86 still committed the open position is -1.57% since entry.

The arithmetic that matters now is the other direction. With 1.99R unused and one position carrying 1.01R, this book could take two more full-risk positions tomorrow. What it should not do is take them because the room exists: the session that created the room also removed the reason to use it, since the complex that every candidate in this book's universe belongs to just printed its worst day of the month. The honest reading of 1.01R against 3.0R is that it is an option, and an option has no expiry here.

What is actually happening at the company you still own

GOOG · 320.76 · next catalyst Q3 earnings, 28 Oct

22 OctFell 3.08% to 320.76, a third consecutive lower close, on volume about 4% above average. Low 318.45. That is through the 328.38 of 9 September, which had been the lowest close of the past two months, and it happened inside the broadest AI de-rating of the month rather than on anything of its own: Meta fell 6.98%, Lam Research about 9%, CoreWeave 10% and the semiconductor index more than 6%.
22 OctThe distinction the market drew is the one that matters for the 28th. Meta funds its data centres out of advertising; Alphabet and Microsoft also rent capacity to outside customers, which is supposed to make the spending self-financing. On Wednesday Pichai said that cloud revenue is being deliberately held back to feed frontier AI. So the one structural defence Alphabet had against Meta's problem is the thing its own chief executive has just qualified, six days before it reports.
21 OctSundar Pichai said Google Cloud is forgoing short-term revenue to make compute trade-offs for frontier AI. On the Big Technology Podcast he called giving DeepMind enough capacity non-negotiable and said taking on new customers who need capacity for next year would be incredibly difficult. He put no number on it and gave no date for when added capacity reaches outside customers. The stock fell 1.62% that day while the Nasdaq rose 1.05%.
20 OctKeyCorp cut its target to $410 from $435 while keeping Overweight, and lead-plaintiff reminders in the securities class action put the deadline at 1 December. The 28 October print carries $195-205bn of capex and now lands the same afternoon as the Fed.

Street: Buy · 44 analysts, average target $421.85 — 31.5% above the 320.76 close.

Wednesday's answer lasted nineteen hours

1. Meta's filing, not Meta's earnings, broke the AI trade. On Wednesday night the numbers looked like a vindication: revenue $64.60bn, up 26%, the 2026 capex floor raised to $135bn, and the shares up about 3% after hours. On Thursday a filing showed future commitments — mostly computing power and data-centre leases — well above their July level, total expense guidance went to $175-179bn, and the stock fell 6.98% to $648.85. Nothing in the results changed. What changed is that the market read the balance-sheet commitment rather than the income statement, and decided that $34.9bn of quarterly capex producing negative $2.12bn of free cash flow is a liability and not an investment. Meta ended the quarter with $82.4bn of cash against $83.7bn of debt, and the chief financial officer said there were no financing plans to announce.

2. And the distinction the market drew is the one Alphabet has to answer on the 28th. Meta funds its data centres out of advertising. Alphabet and Microsoft also rent capacity to outside customers, which is the structural defence: the spending is supposed to arrive back as cloud revenue. Except that on Wednesday Pichai said that cloud revenue is being deliberately held back to give DeepMind capacity, with new customers next year incredibly difficult. So the defence has been qualified by the company that owns it, six days before it reports. Alphabet fell 3.08% and Microsoft 1.5% while the semiconductor index fell more than 6% and Lam Research 9% on weak guidance. The chain is coherent: if the hyperscalers' spending is a liability, the people selling them equipment have a demand problem.

3. The bond market took the other side, and France went past the United States. The ten-year fell about 18 basis points to 4.95%, its largest one-day drop since August 2025, with the two-year down about 16 and the thirty-year 13. Hike odds for next week fell to about 10.5%. That is not an inflation trade — crude rose 2.4% on the same afternoon — it is money leaving equity risk and a growth scare being priced, with jobless claims at 194,000, a three-month low, ruling out the labour market as the cause. Meanwhile the French ten-year rose 6bp to 5.06%, a 24-year high, and crossed above the US ten-year for the first time since 2013. This brief spent Monday to Wednesday establishing that French politics does not move American yields. Thursday confirmed it from the opposite direction: the two curves moved apart as far as they have in thirteen years, in a single session, for entirely unrelated reasons.

The strikes now have a date, and it is after the midterms

The New York Times reported that the United States and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the 3 November midterms. The reported target set is energy sites, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenals, with the report allowing a small chance that it happens this month. Trump said the US is not negotiating with Iran and that something will happen fairly soon; a separate report had the Israeli chief of staff seeing no operational need to strike before the election. That is the first time this conflict has had a date attached to it, and a dated war is a different instrument from an open-ended one — it gives the oil curve something to price rather than something to fear.

Crude priced it immediately. Brent rose $4.35, or 4%, to $113.17 and WTI $2.32, or 2.39%, to $99.47, a five-month high, after touching $100. The other half of the move was physical: an attack on King Fahd International Airport at Dammam killed one resident and injured eight, per Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority, and there were further reported strikes on Saudi energy targets. The IRGC Navy said four oil-carrying vessels were hit and caught fire in the northern Persian Gulf, and three more struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, and warned that continued US escorting of ships through the Strait could bring responses against American regional bases.

And then the strangest line of the day. Trump accused Iran of making up fake hits on ships to drive up oil prices ahead of the midterms. Take it seriously as market information rather than as rhetoric: it is an American president publicly asserting that part of the war premium in the oil price is fabricated, eight days after signing an order waiving sanctions on Russian energy to hold fuel prices down, and twelve days before an election. Whether or not the claim is true, it tells you the energy line in the inflation data is now being managed as a political variable, and that the administration's tolerance for a hundred-dollar barrel before 3 November is low.

For this book the transmission has changed shape. A fortnight ago crude rising meant yields rising, and that was the whole mechanism — energy into inflation into the long end into everything. On Thursday crude rose 2.4% and the ten-year fell 18 basis points. The bond market has stopped treating the oil shock as an inflation problem and started treating it as a demand one, which is the same conclusion the housing data forced on Tuesday. Gold fell 2.81% on the same afternoon, which only makes sense if the market is pricing growth damage rather than price pressure. If that holds, the energy premium stops being the thing that threatens this book's valuations and becomes the thing that threatens its earnings.

weekly.headline: The worst week since June for the Nasdaq — and the Dow was the only index that rose
weekly.standfirst: Two hot inflation prints and the long end fell through both of them. September CPI came in +0.6% on the month and +3.7% on the year and September PPI at +1.3% against +0.5% expected — yet the ten-year finished the week about 14 basis points lower and the thirty-year 17 lower at 5.43%, with hike odds for 28 October ending near 27% after touching 50%. The explanation is the retail sales control group at +0.1% against +0.3% expected: gasoline did over half of CPI, rose 20.3% at the producer level and supplied most of the retail beat, so the market read it as a tax on demand. The Nasdaq fell 4.5% and the S&P 1.9%, both their worst week since June; the Russell fell 3% at three weekly sigma; and the Dow rose 0.7%, the only index up. Crude broke $100, from $90.76 to $101.41, through roughly 37m barrels of announced emergency release. Four of six instruments had a move of more than one weekly sigma, and the ranking is the whole week. The Russell fell 3.05% at 3.17σ — the largest weekly reading on this board in the series. The Nasdaq fell 4.48% at 1.99σ, crude rose 11.73% at 1.85σ and the S&P fell 1.95% at 1.69σ. And then the two that did nothing: the Dow rose 0.67% at 0.63σ and gold fell 0.20% at 0.13σ. A week in which the small-cap index has its most unusual move of the series, the Nasdaq has its worst week since June, crude rises eleven percent and gold does not move at all is not a week with one story in it.

The indices, precisely. Across the five sessions the S&P fell 152.10 points, or 1.9%, to 7,659.44; the Nasdaq 1,226.14, or 4.5%, to 26,140.03 — its worst week since June, as was the S&P's; the Russell 85.61, or 3%, to 2,721.37. The Dow rose 347.46 points, or 0.7%, to 52,002.41, and was the only index up. For the year the S&P is now up 11.9%, the Nasdaq 12.5%, the Russell 9.6% and the Dow 8.2% — the Dow has closed almost the whole of the gap the Nasdaq built over the first nine months.

Two first-tier prints, both hot, and the long end fell anyway. September CPI on Wednesday came in +0.6% on the month and +3.7% on the year, core +0.3% and +2.6%, both above forecast — with gasoline +9.1% and +34.2% doing over half the monthly increase on the BLS's own reckoning, and shelter and core services both accelerating to +0.4%. September PPI on Thursday came in at +1.3% against +0.5% expected, +6.3% on the year, with energy goods +10.8% and gasoline +20.3% at the producer level. Hike odds for 28 October went from about 22% to roughly 50% to about 27% inside three sessions. And the ten-year finished the week about 14 basis points lower and the thirty-year about 17, at 5.43%. Fed Chair Warsh's IMF remarks left roughly an 85% hold priced for this month.

The number that explains it is in the retail sales report, not the inflation ones. Headline retail sales rose 0.8% against 0.3% expected, to $745.0bn. But the control group rose only 0.1% against 0.3% expected, and excluding petrol stations the increase was 0.2%. So the consumer is not spending more; the consumer is paying more for fuel. Gasoline did over half of CPI, rose a fifth at the producer level, and supplied most of the retail beat. The bond market read that as a tax on demand rather than inflation to be met with hikes, and bought duration into two hot prints. That is the single most important thing the week established.

And crude broke a hundred dollars. WTI went from $90.76 to $101.41, +11.7%, and Brent from $103.35 to $109.86, touching $110 on Friday for the first time since May. Gold finished the week almost exactly where it started, at $4,166.39, having fallen 1.34% on the CPI and risen 1.60% on the PPI. An eleven-percent week in oil and a flat week in gold is a market pricing a supply problem, not a monetary one.

The worst week of the stretch — and the R column is the part to read

The percentage and dollar columns above are the week, 12 to 16 October. The R column is where each position stands against the risk it was opened with. The book moved -83.62 across the five sessions and now shows +37.07 open at +1.81R. One position closed: AMZN was stopped out on Wednesday the 15th, gapping through its breakeven stop at the open, realising -2.85 or -0.14R — and costing -34.62 measured from the previous Friday's close. The nearest line on the week's lows was GOOG, 8.89% above its 305.67 stop. Heat is 3.05R against a 3.0R cap (2.04R excluding the managed GOOG position) and has not moved since 14 September.

OKTA is the week. It fell 19.3% across five consecutive losing sessions, from 232.13 to 187.26, taking −44.87 out of the book — more than half the week's loss on its own. On Monday it opened at 235.00, a 52-week high; by Friday it had fallen 10.20% in a single session, the largest of its life. The position has gone from +2.46R to +0.23R. There was no company news in any of the five sessions. What there was instead: a stock up 152.4% on the year, one screen calling it 102.4% above intrinsic value, $54.8m of insider selling over twelve months, and agent revenue not forecast to begin until fiscal 2028. The 5 October valuation note has now largely been settled against the position.

AAPL was the only thing that worked, and only at the end. It rose 2.0% across the week while the Nasdaq fell 4.5%, and at +1.04R it is the only position left above +1R, carrying 58% of the open profit. The week's argument about iPhone demand ran through three contradictory supply-chain reports and was then settled on Friday by the only checkable event in it: the iPhone Duo sold out within moments of pre-orders opening, Apple called the demand nothing short of extraordinary, shipping slipped to late January 2027 on some configurations, and units resold at up to $5,000 against a $1,999 list. GOOG, meanwhile, fell 3.2% to +0.55R, its lowest close since 2 October.

And the AMZN exit is the week's lesson, stated once. The stop was at the fill, 251.84, which made the position riskless in the sense that mattered: no capital could be lost. It did not make the fill riskless. On Wednesday the stock gapped to a 250.89 open, ninety-five cents below the stop, with no trade in between — so the exit was the open, not the stop, and the trade realised -2.85 instead of nothing. It then fell to 248.65 and closed 254.76, above the stop. In a $250 stock that can gap three dollars overnight, a breakeven stop means risk of about a dollar a share, and the position most likely to be taken out is the one with the tightest line regardless of how safe that line looks. Heat did not fall when it closed, either — a stop at the entry was carrying no risk, so removing it freed none.

Where the quarter stands · twelve sessions in

Q4 is +34.22 at +1.67R, of which -2.85 is realised and the rest is open profit accrued since entry — not a Q4 return. Q3 finished at +12.31, +0.58R, against the S&P's +2.0%. On $830.56 of capital still committed the open book is +4.46% since entry. The week cost -83.62 against an S&P down 1.9%, a Nasdaq down 4.5% and a Dow up 0.7%, which is the comparison that matters: 1 of the 3 positions is above +1R (AAPL at +1.04R), and the index this book owns nothing in was the only one that rose.

Two hot prints, a bank fine, a foldable sell-out, and a rotation that completed

1. The long end fell through two hot inflation prints, and that settles a three-week argument. The thesis built from 29 September was that the long end was rising on supply and global debt rather than inflation. This week tested it to destruction: the ten-year spiked to 5.33% on the CPI and closed back at 5.19%; then fell 12 basis points on the PPI to a three-week low; and finished the week about 14 basis points lower, with the thirty-year 17 lower at 5.43%. Neither explanation survives. An inflation trade would have risen and stayed risen. A pure supply trade would not have spiked on CPI at all. What fits is the retail sales control group at +0.1%: the market read energy-driven price rises as demand destruction and bought duration into them. Hike odds for 28 October ended the week near 27% after touching 50%.

2. The banks reported and the split told you where the cycle is. JPMorgan missed for the first time in nearly three years — $5.57 against $5.93 expected — on investment banking and a fixed-income desk that slowed from the summer. Goldman earned $17.01 against $12.25 a year ago on stock trading, with bond trading slower. Citigroup's profit rose 40% but card profits were flat. Bank of America missed on Wednesday — $0.91 a share including a charge, $1.08 against $1.10 excluding it, revenue $30bn against $30.58bn, investment banking fees −11% and sales and trading −5% — the day after the Treasury fined it $1.2bn, the third-largest penalty in that department's history, for willful Bank Secrecy Act violations involving more than $5bn of suspicious transactions. The pattern: equity desks busy, bond desks quiet, consumer flat.

3. Apple's foldable sold out in minutes, which was the only checkable fact in a fortnight of sourcing. Three parties had disagreed from anonymous supply-chain contacts — Nikkei on iPhone 18 Pro cuts, Securities Times on Duo orders raised 30% toward ten million units, Bank of America on shorter Pro delivery times — and Friday replaced all of it with evidence. Pre-orders opened at 8am Eastern, stock went within moments, shipping slipped to late January 2027 on some configurations, Apple called demand nothing short of extraordinary, and units resold at up to $5,000 against a $1,999 list. The fair caveat is that a sell-out is a ratio and Apple probably built few of them. The resale premium is harder to argue with.

4. And the rotation completed, which is the week's real lesson for this book. Over five sessions the Dow rose 0.7% and was the only index up, while the Nasdaq fell 4.5% and the Russell 3%. Friday's sell-off is the one to study: the Nasdaq fell 2.15% and the Dow 0.34% while the ten-year rose two basis points. That was not a rate event. Micron fell 5.6% and Intel 5.8% as investors grew more concerned about how long AI infrastructure spending will last, and Okta, Palantir, Datadog, Zscaler and Elastic were sold together. A rate scare reverses when the Fed is repriced — and it did, on Thursday. A thesis under question does not.

Crude rose eleven percent through two emergency releases

WTI went from $90.76 to $101.41 across the week, up 11.7%, and Brent touched $110 on Friday for the first time since May. It did so through four separate supply events and against the two largest tools short of policy that the agencies have. Monday: +3.28% on renewed Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Tuesday: WTI up, Brent down, as traders weighed a possible US–Russia diesel deal against escalation in Yemen. Wednesday: +1.01% after a Houthi missile hit an office tower at Aramco's Dhahran headquarters — top three floors damaged, limited fire, no injuries, a command centre rather than a producing asset. Thursday: +3.03% on a US inventory draw. Friday: +3.51%.

Friday's reasons are worth separating because one of them is new. A Saudi-led coalition intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Yanbu — the Red Sea export terminal whose entire strategic value is that crude leaving from it bypasses the Strait of Hormuz. Targeting the hedge against the chokepoint is an escalation in kind, not degree. Ukrainian strikes also damaged the Ryazan refinery, shutting a primary crude unit, which bears directly on Russian diesel. And the EIA reported US crude stocks down 8.6m barrels to 415.6m, with distillates down 2.5m.

Against all of which: the IEA announced the release of over 20m barrels of emergency supply, and Washington offered up to 17m through a reserve exchange. Roughly 37m barrels of announced additional supply, and the price rose 3.5% on the day and 11.7% on the week. The reason is the number Aramco's Amin Nasser has been repeating: commercial inventory under 6 billion barrels against roughly 10 billion before the crisis, with less than 10% practically available and up to two years to rebuild. A release needs a cushion to land on. There is not one.

And the diesel number is how all of this reaches a book with no oil position in it. The IEA reported combined net gasoil exports from the Middle East and Russia down 1.3m barrels a day in September to 820,000 — more than 60% lower year on year — with no stock rebuild expected before the second half of 2027, because the binding constraint is how much Russian refining capacity is actually running. Gulf crude exports are back at 13.9m barrels a day, over 75% of pre-war; refined product exports are 1.9m against 4.7m. Crude flows and product does not. That gap is why gasoline rose 20.3% at the producer level in September and did over half of the CPI increase — and the October print, due 10 November, carries a crude price eleven percent higher than when this week began.

Ten days of empty calendar, then four events in three days

There is nothing dated for ten days, and that has not been true since late September. No print, no earnings, no scheduled event from any company held, until the Duo ships on Friday 23 October. Then the calendar compresses: the Fed and Alphabet on Wednesday the 28th, Apple and Amazon on Thursday the 29th, Palantir on 2 November and October CPI on the 10th. Four of the five positions this book has held during October report inside those three days.

Alphabet on the 28th is the one that has changed character. A fortnight ago its $195-205bn of capex and the 3.6-gigawatt Constellation deal were the bull case — evidence of scale. After a Friday in which Micron fell 5.6% and Intel 5.8% because investors are no longer sure how long AI infrastructure spending lasts, the same number is the thing the print has to defend. And it lands the same afternoon the Fed decides, so two factors resolve on one day for a book exposed to both.

What to watch in this book. Whether AAPL holds what the pre-order gave it — at +1.04R it is the only position above +1R and carries 58% of the open profit, a concentration that arrived by subtraction. Whether OKTA finds a floor at +0.23R after nineteen percent in five sessions. And whether GOOG can hold 335 into its own print. All of them now turn on one question, and it is no longer the Fed: whether the market still believes the AI build.

The standing position: do nothing, because nothing can be done. Heat is 3.05R against a 3.0R cap and has not moved in twenty-seven sessions, so no position can be added however attractive anything looks. This week was the first real test of that constraint: two holdings fell more than ten percent, one closed, and the book could not respond to any of it. The ten days to the 23rd are the first stretch since September with nothing to react to, which makes them the right time to decide what this book should look like when it can act again.
